Gold added about $109 an ounce in twenty-four hours, and not one ounce of it came out of a mine.

At 5:58am New York on Wednesday gold was bid $4,157.80, up 1.99%; silver $61.35, up 3.27%; platinum $1,747.00, up 1.10%; palladium $1,355.00, up 1.96%. Third session up for all four. Against the $4,048.80 this paper carried on Tuesday, gold has put on roughly $109.

The cause is a shipping lane. The United States, Iran and Oman are reported closing on an interim deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Oil fell on the expectation, the September Fed hike odds went to about 57% from 67%, and gold rose because the war premium is coming out, not because it is going in.

For the bench the number is the gram, not the ounce: $133.68 a gram of fine gold against $130.17 yesterday. That is $3.51 added to the metal cost of every piece in the case overnight, and the gold to silver ratio tightened to 67.8 from 69.0.

Two cautions belong on the record. The intraday spread was wide — our own overnight print was $4,170.90 at 3:08am — so a reader working from a headline number rather than a timestamp is working from the wrong number. And Trading Economics printed platinum and palladium $13.10 and $17.00 above Kitco, which is this paper's designated mark.

The diamond industry's marketing body has stopped advertising to the diamond industry.

Amber Pepper, chief executive of the Natural Diamond Council, told a GJEPC meeting in Mumbai on Monday that at least 80% of the council's advertising spend now goes to consumers rather than to the trade — the category that talks to people who already sell diamonds. The budget is up significantly on last year; the figure was not given.

Three instruments came with it. A Diamond Desire Index tracking consideration, purchase intent, sentiment and recommendation across India, China and the United States, with a baseline due in September 2026. A Natural Diamond Mark, to be inscribed on natural stones and jewellery globally. And six pillars, from category marketing to how natural diamonds appear inside large language models, where a growing share of pre-purchase research now happens.

The arithmetic it is aimed at has not moved much. De Beers' consolidated average realised price fell 32% across the first half to $105 a carat, and the 1-carat polished index only stopped falling in July after thirteen months down.

The mark is the more interesting half. A category losing to a chemically identical product at a fraction of the price has two defences, provenance and meaning, and an inscribed mark is the only one you can verify at a counter. Retailers should ask now what it costs, who applies it, and whether it appears on goods already in the safe.

Luk Fook's record year has been public since June, and the number that explains it has not travelled.

In the twelve months to 31 March the Hong Kong group's net profit rose 88.7% to HK$2.015 billion, its highest on record, on revenue up 29% to HK$17.21 billion and a gross margin of 36.7%. The English pickups compressed that to a profit-growth headline. The Cantonese and Mandarin financial press carried the driver.

The driver is the mix. Sales of fixed-price jewellery, priced by the piece, rose 50.5%. Sales of gold and platinum priced by weight rose 22%. A weight-priced chain passes the metal cost straight to the customer and earns the retailer a labour charge on top. A fixed-price piece carries the margin inside the ticket. With gold at a record, the weight-priced case is where sticker shock lands and the fixed-price case is where the margin survives.

The risk is the same shape as the reward. Fixed-price merchandise caps the revenue upside when volume returns, it demands design and brand strength that weight-selling does not, and it has to be bought forward — which moves the metal exposure from the shop floor to the hedging desk.

Every independent watching gold pass $4,150 an ounce is facing the identical problem. Luk Fook's answer is the most transferable idea in Asian retail jewellery this year, and most of the English-speaking trade has not read it.
